title: Implement data operations in Azure Managed Redis

questions.q: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?

options.text: The app returns an error and retries later
options.why: A miss isn't an error.

options.text: Redis forwards the request to the database by itself
options.why: The application, not Redis, reads the database.

options.text: The app reads the database, then caches the result
options.why: Correct. Data is loaded into the cache only when requested.

options.text: Redis loads the entire database into memory
options.why: Cache-aside avoids preloading whole datasets.

questions.hint: Cache-aside loads data into the cache only when it's asked for.
questions.explain: Check Redis first; on a miss, fetch from the database and cache it for next time.

questions.q: An inference API needs the highest Redis throughput and has modest memory needs. Which tier fits?

options.text: Balanced (4:1)
options.why: Balanced is for standard workloads.

options.text: Memory Optimized (8:1)
options.why: Memory Optimized favors memory over throughput.

options.text: Compute Optimized (2:1)
options.why: Correct. Compute Optimized is for performance-intensive workloads needing maximum throughput.

options.text: Flash Optimized (preview)
options.why: Flash Optimized trades performance for cheaper large datasets.

questions.hint: Highest throughput with modest memory: the tier with the lowest memory-to-vCPU ratio.
questions.explain: Match the memory-to-vCPU ratio to the workload.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A web app stores shopping carts and preferences in cookies, and pages have become slow.

rows.text: Large cookies are sent with every HTTP request and response, adding bandwidth and latency.
rows.why: Storing too much in cookies hurts performance.

rows.text: Keeping only a session id in the cookie and the data in Redis is the typical fix.
rows.why: The session id is the key to the session data in Redis.

rows.text: Azure Managed Redis can only be used by applications hosted in Azure.
rows.why: It's usable by any application inside or outside Azure.

questions.hint: Cookies travel with every request. Keep only an id in the cookie.
questions.explain: The session store pattern keeps cookies small and session data in memory.

questions.q: A team must cache a very large product dataset where most items are rarely read, and cost matters more than peak speed. Which tier fits?

options.text: Balanced
options.why: Balanced keeps everything in memory at a higher cost for this size.

options.text: Compute Optimized
options.why: Compute Optimized has the least memory per vCPU.

options.text: Flash Optimized (preview)
options.why: Correct. It moves less-used data from RAM to NVMe for cost-effective large caches.

options.text: Memory Optimized with high availability disabled
options.why: Disabling HA doesn't change where data is stored; Learn says keep HA on in production.

questions.hint: Big dataset, mostly cold, cost first: the tier that moves cold data to NVMe.
questions.explain: Flash Optimized trades some performance for scaling large datasets cheaply.

questions.q: A development team needs a Redis cache for testing with lots of memory, and it doesn't need high throughput. They want the lowest price point. Which tier fits?

options.text: Memory Optimized (8:1 memory-to-vCPU)
options.why: Correct. Memory Optimized suits memory-intensive use without top throughput, at a lower price, which is good for dev and test.

options.text: Compute Optimized (2:1 memory-to-vCPU)
options.why: This is for maximum throughput, which the team doesn't need.

options.text: Flash Optimized (preview)
options.why: Flash moves cold data to NVMe for very large datasets. It isn't the dev/test default.

options.text: Balanced (4:1 memory-to-vCPU)
options.why: Balanced is the standard choice for production workloads, not the lowest price for memory.

questions.hint: Lots of memory and little compute means a high memory-to-vCPU ratio.
questions.explain: Memory Optimized (8:1) suits memory-intensive workloads that don't need top throughput, with a lower price point that's good for dev/test. Balanced (4:1) is for standard workloads; Compute Optimized (2:1) for maximum throughput.

questions.q: Every page on a retail site renders the same header, footer, banners and navigation menu from templates, which takes time on each request. Which Redis caching use case fits?

options.text: Message queue
options.why: Queues hand work between processes. They don't serve repeated page content.

options.text: Content cache
options.why: Correct. Static template content such as headers and footers rarely changes, so it's ideal to cache.

options.text: Rate limiter
options.why: Rate limiting counts requests. It doesn't speed up page rendering.

options.text: Session store
options.why: A session store holds per-user data such as carts, not shared page fragments.

questions.hint: The data is the same for everyone and rarely changes.
questions.explain: Content cache: static template content (headers, footers, banners, navigation) rarely changes and is ideal for Redis, giving sub-millisecond access and reducing web server load.

questions.q: A cleanup job needs to find all keys matching `user:42:*` in production. Which command should it use?

options.text: KEYS `user:42:*` on the primary
options.why: KEYS is expensive and blocks; don't use it in production.

options.text: SCAN with a match pattern
options.why: Correct. SCAN iterates keys without blocking the server.

options.text: FLUSHDB, then reload the data
options.why: FLUSHDB deletes everything.

options.text: CLUSTER KEYSLOT for each key
options.why: That's blocked and doesn't list keys.

questions.hint: One command blocks the server while it walks every key. Use the one that iterates in steps.
questions.explain: Avoid expensive operations: use SCAN instead of KEYS.

questions.q: Which Python client library does Learn list for Azure Managed Redis?

options.text: Lettuce
options.why: That's the Java client.

options.text: StackExchange.Redis
options.why: That's the C#/.NET client.

options.text: redis-py
options.why: Correct. redis-py is the Python client.

options.text: node_redis
options.why: That's the Node.js client.

questions.hint: The Python client's name is redis followed by the language's short name.
questions.explain: StackExchange.Redis (.NET), Lettuce (Java), node_redis (Node.js), redis-py (Python).

questions.q: An app uses MSET across keys in different hash slots and gets CROSSSLOT errors. The instance uses the OSS clustering policy. What's the fix?

options.text: Switch the command from MSET to MGET
options.why: MGET is also multi-key and has the same constraint.

options.text: Make the keys map to the same hash slot
options.why: Correct. With OSS clustering, all keys in a multi-key command must map to the same hash slot.

options.text: Enable Active-Active geo-replication on it
options.why: Active-Active restricts cross-slot commands further.

options.text: Run KEYS before MSET to find each key's slot
options.why: KEYS is expensive and doesn't fix slot mapping.

questions.hint: With OSS clustering, multi-key commands need every key in the same hash slot.
questions.explain: Enterprise clustering allows some multi-key commands across slots; OSS clustering doesn't.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A database uses Enterprise clustering with Active-Active geo-replication.

rows.why: In Active-Active databases, MGET, EXISTS and TOUCH work across slots.

rows.text: DEL across hash slots works the same as without geo-replication.
rows.why: In Active-Active, only MGET, EXISTS and TOUCH work across slots.

rows.text: FLUSHALL is available to clear the cache quickly.
rows.why: FLUSHALL and FLUSHDB are blocked for active geo-replication.

questions.hint: Active-Active narrows which multi-key commands work across slots and blocks the flush commands.
questions.explain: Active-Active narrows which commands you can use.

questions.q: Which two practices does Learn recommend for connecting to Azure Managed Redis? (Select two.)

options.text: Connect with the hostname rather than the public IP
options.why: Correct. IP addresses can change during scale operations.

options.text: Disable TLS on the connection to reduce latency
options.why: TLS is required by default (1.2 and 1.3).

options.text: Connect to the public IP so that DNS isn't needed
options.why: Public IPs can change; use hostnames.

options.text: Place Redis and the app in the same Azure region
options.why: Correct. Co-locating reduces latency.

questions.hint: Keep the app close to the cache, and don't rely on an IP that can change.
questions.explain: Co-locate, use hostnames, keep TLS on; scale when metrics stay above 75%.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A database uses the Enterprise clustering policy without geo-replication.

rows.why: Enterprise clustering allows DEL, MSET, MGET, EXISTS, UNLINK and TOUCH across slots.

rows.text: CLUSTER NODES can be used to inspect the topology.
rows.why: CLUSTER INFO, HELP, KEYSLOT, NODES and SLOTS are blocked with Enterprise clustering.

rows.text: Every client library can connect to this database.
rows.why: All client libraries work with the Enterprise clustering policy.

questions.hint: Enterprise clustering hides the cluster from clients. Think about what that allows and what it blocks.
questions.explain: With Enterprise clustering, all client libraries work, and DEL, MSET, MGET, EXISTS, UNLINK and TOUCH work across slots. CLUSTER INFO/HELP/KEYSLOT/NODES/SLOTS are blocked. Active-Active narrows cross-slot commands to MGET, EXISTS and TOUCH.

questions.q: An app caches each user's full 4 MB recommendation payload under one key, and responses are slow under load. Which best practice does Learn give first?

options.text: Turn off TLS to make the payload smaller
options.why: TLS is required, and it doesn't change payload size.

options.text: Move the cache to a different region from the app
options.why: Placing the cache in the same region as the app is the recommendation.

options.text: Split the data into several keys with smaller values
options.why: Correct. Use smaller values and divide large chunks across multiple keys.

options.text: Use KEYS to find and delete the large values
options.why: KEYS is an expensive command that shouldn't be used in production.

questions.hint: Redis works best with many small values.
questions.explain: Best practices: use smaller values (divide large data into multiple keys), use pipelining, avoid KEYS (use SCAN), co-locate in one region, use hostnames, and keep TLS on.

questions.q: Your production cache's Used Memory Percentage has stayed around 80% for two weeks, and CPU is at 78%. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Disable high availability to free memory
options.why: High availability should stay on in production.

options.text: Scale the instance, because the metrics consistently exceed 75%
options.why: Correct. Learn says to scale when key metrics consistently exceed 75%.

options.text: Wait until memory reaches 100%, because eviction handles the rest
options.why: Running near capacity risks evictions and latency. Learn's threshold is 75%.

options.text: Run FLUSHALL weekly to keep memory low
options.why: Flushing deletes all data, which defeats the cache.

questions.hint: Learn gives one percentage threshold for memory, CPU, clients and bandwidth.
questions.explain: Monitor Used Memory Percentage, CPU, Connected Clients and Network bandwidth, and scale when they consistently exceed 75%.

questions.q: To cut costs, a teammate proposes disabling high availability on the production cache that holds user sessions. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Disable it and enable Flash Optimized instead
options.why: Flash Optimized is about storage cost, not availability.

options.text: Keep high availability on in production; disable it only for dev or test
options.why: Correct. Use high availability for production workloads.

options.text: Disable it, because Redis data is always rebuilt from the database
options.why: Sessions may not be in any database, and an outage would log users out.

options.text: Disable it, but turn on data persistence to replace it
options.why: Persistence helps recovery. It isn't a replacement for high availability.

questions.hint: It's production data that users depend on.
questions.explain: Enable high availability for production workloads and only disable it for dev/test. For data protection, add data persistence or periodic import/export.

questions.q: A Python app connects to Azure Managed Redis with redis-py. Which port should it use?

options.why: Learn doesn't list 6379 for these services.
6380 is for Azure Cache for Redis instances.
443 isn't the Redis port here.
Correct. Azure Managed Redis and Enterprise caches use port 10000.

questions.hint: Azure Managed Redis listens on a different port from the older Azure Cache for Redis.
questions.explain: Azure Managed Redis: 10000; Azure Cache for Redis: 6380.

questions.q: A rate limiter counts requests per user across many API instances and must avoid race conditions. Which command fits?

options.text: INCR on a per-user key
options.why: Correct. INCR is atomic, so concurrent increments don't conflict.

options.text: GET then SET with the new value
options.why: Read-then-write can race between instances.

options.text: HSET on a per-user field
options.why: HSET overwrites a field; it doesn't increment atomically here.

options.text: LPUSH to a per-user list
options.why: A list grows with entries rather than counting atomically.

questions.hint: Counting across many instances needs an atomic operation.
questions.explain: INCR, DECR, INCRBY and DECRBY are atomic counters.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You store a user profile with `r.hset('user:1001', mapping={...})` and want it to expire in one hour.

rows.text: SETEX can store the hash and set its expiry in one command.
rows.why: SETEX is for string values; for hashes, set the data then use EXPIRE.
EXPIRE works on keys of any type.

rows.text: If r.ttl('user:1001') returns -1, the key exists but has no expiry.
rows.why: -1 means no expiration; -2 means the key doesn't exist.

rows.text: If r.ttl('user:1001') returns -2, the key exists with no expiry.
rows.why: -2 means the key doesn't exist; -1 means no expiry.

questions.hint: SETEX is for strings. Hashes get their expiry separately. Learn the TTL return codes.
questions.explain: Expiry commands operate on keys, so they work with every data type.

questions.q: An instance uses the OSS clustering policy, and code built with `redis.Redis(...)` fails on keys in other slots. What should the Python code use?

options.text: redis.Redis with port 6380
options.why: 6380 is the Azure Cache for Redis port and doesn't address clustering.

options.text: redis.Redis with decode_responses=False
options.why: decode_responses only changes byte/string handling.

options.text: redis.cluster.RedisCluster
options.why: Correct. With OSS clustering, connect with redis.cluster.RedisCluster.

options.text: redis.asyncio.Redis
options.why: The async client doesn't change clustering support.

questions.hint: With OSS clustering, the client must understand the cluster.
questions.explain: The clustering policy changes how you connect: OSS needs a cluster-aware client.

questions.q: Match each cached item to Learn's suggested TTL range.

items.text: Live stock levels that change constantly
Product recommendations that change a few times a day

questions.hint: The more often data changes, the shorter its TTL.
questions.explain: Balance data freshness against cache hit rate when choosing TTLs.

questions.q: An app caches pickled Python objects in Redis. After the connection is created with decode_responses=True, reading them back fails. What should you change?

options.text: Use decode_responses=False for binary data such as pickled objects
options.why: Correct. decode_responses=True converts responses to strings, which breaks binary data.

options.text: Connect on port 6380 instead of 10000
options.why: The port is about which service you connect to, not decoding.

options.text: Store the objects with HSET instead of SET
options.why: The data type doesn't fix the decoding of binary values.

options.text: Add an expiry to each key
options.why: Expiry controls lifetime, not how values are decoded.

questions.hint: One connection option turns bytes into text automatically.
questions.explain: decode_responses=True converts byte responses to strings, which suits text. For binary data such as images or pickled objects, use decode_responses=False.

questions.q: A production app should stop using an access key and connect to Azure Managed Redis with Microsoft Entra ID. What does Learn point to for redis-py?

options.text: redis.cluster.RedisCluster, which handles authentication
options.why: RedisCluster is for OSS clustering. It doesn't add Entra ID authentication.

options.text: The redis-entraid package, with a token for https://redis.azure.com/.default
options.why: Correct. redis-entraid adds Entra ID authentication to redis-py.

options.text: Port 6380 with TLS turned off
options.why: Azure Managed Redis uses port 10000, and TLS is required.

options.text: A password set to the app's client ID
options.why: A client ID isn't a credential, and Entra ID authentication uses tokens.

questions.hint: Entra ID support for redis-py comes from an add-on library.
questions.explain: For production, use Microsoft Entra ID authentication with the redis-entraid package, requesting tokens for https://redis.azure.com/.default.

questions.q: Background workers must process inference jobs in the order they were submitted (first in, first out). Which Redis data type and commands fit?

options.text: A List, adding with LPUSH and taking with RPOP
options.why: Correct. Lists are ordered, and pushing on one end while popping from the other gives a FIFO queue.

options.text: A List, adding with LPUSH and taking with LPOP
options.why: Pushing and popping on the same end gives LIFO (a stack), not FIFO.

options.text: A Hash, adding with HSET and reading with HGETALL
options.why: Hashes hold field-value pairs with no order for processing.

options.text: A String counter, using INCR for each job
options.why: A counter tracks a number. It doesn't hold the jobs.

questions.hint: Lists can act as a stack or a queue, depending on which ends you use.
questions.explain: Redis Lists are ordered collections. LPUSH/RPUSH add to either end and LPOP/RPOP remove; using opposite ends gives a FIFO queue, the same end gives LIFO.

questions.q: A team stores each field of a product (name, price, category, rating) as a separate key, such as product:42:name. Memory use is higher than expected. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Serialize every product into one giant string key
options.why: Very large values are discouraged, and you'd lose per-field access.

options.text: Use MSET so that the separate keys take less space
options.why: MSET writes several keys at once, but it doesn't make them smaller.

options.text: Store each product as one Hash with HSET
options.why: Correct. Hashes keep field-value pairs in one key and are more memory-efficient than separate keys.

options.text: Store each field as a List element
options.why: Lists are for ordered collections, not named fields.

questions.hint: One data type holds an object's fields under a single key.
questions.explain: Hashes store objects as field-value pairs within a single key (HSET, HGET, HGETALL) and are more memory-efficient than storing each field as a separate key.
